title: Financial services: Diversa may have charged fees on 'non-existent' super balances: ASIC
full_text:
The corporate regulator is investigating whether superannuation trustee Diversa inappropriately charged fees to victims of the First Guardian collapse even after their retirement savings were written down to nothing, in the watchdog's third major probe into the controversial company.
The disclosure to Senator Deborah O'Neill's joint parliamentary committee for financial services followed a fiery appearance by Diversa executives and chairman Vincent Plant.
Plant said the company had no guarantees from its private equity shareholders that they would continue to support the business and protect the company from insolvency if it was forced to repay nearly $250 million to victims of the First Guardian investment scheme.
Plant also defended the board's decision to award chief executive Andrew Peterson a $770,000 bonus despite the First Guardian failure and shortcomings in Diversa's own governance systems, in comments that met with audible incredulity from some politicians on the committee.
Diversa had drawn sharp scrutiny after the collapse. Regulators conducted several investigations and imposed onerous licence conditions on the company due to its exposure to the failed scheme.
The trustee hosted First Guardian on investment platforms that it was responsible for. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has alleged that up to $300 million was invested in the scheme through Diversa's systems, with victims lured out of large superannuation funds by dodgy financial advisers and lead generators.
ASIC sued the company, alleging it did not properly review First Guardian before making it available for investment, should have recognised red flags of potentially fraudulent behaviour and introduced better protections for members. Diversa is defending the claims and argued it was the role of platform operator Praemium, not the trustee, to ensure the products were suitable for investment.
ASIC enforcement head Chris Savundra, who appeared after Plant, said the regulator was investigating whether Diversa had inappropriately charged fees to victims of the scheme even after it had written the value of First Guardian to zero. Stressing that the probe was in a "case theory" stage, Savundra said ASIC was looking at the timing of Diversa's decision to write off First Guardian compared to when that was reflected in member balances.
"[The deferment] may have resulted in members being charged fees based on the last strike unit price of First Guardian," he said. "What that means is members who had already seen most of their superannuation eroded by the collapse of First Guardian were still being charged fees on the basis of a non-existent asset value."
ASIC also started investigating how Diversa billed its largest clients after persistent complaints it did not offer sufficient explanations for fees and blocked efforts from client funds to find a new third-party trustee provider.
ASIC chairman Sarah Court also criticised Diversa's characterisation that it was "working with ASIC" during the hearing. "Diversa is getting sued by ASIC; that is not working with ASIC," she said.
Plant said Diversa was "acutely aware" of the toll First Guardian's failure had on members, but had discharged its responsibilities fully and was not ultimately liable for the losses. Diversa applied to the government for a taxpayer bailout to compensate victims. "No one can predict in advance a fraud. We are not clairvoyant," Plant said.
The explanation was rejected by O'Neill and Liberal senator Paul Scarr, who pointed out that other regulators also imposed licence conditions on Diversa over its involvement in the scheme's collapse, citing concerns about its due diligence and onboarding of new investment options.
"You've got obligations in respect to due diligence, you have responsibility in terms of monitoring and you certainly have responsibility on holding limits. The taxpayer is not there to be a guarantor for trustees that do not discharge their obligations," Scarr said.
O'Neill described Diversa's approach as "all profit, no responsibility".
Scarr asked how Diversa could defend ASIC's claims when the regulator had already secured agreements from similarly exposed trustees Macquarie Group and Netwealth that their processes had failed when onboarding First Guardian and the failed Shield scheme. Both trustees had since compensated victims. In response, Plant clarified that the trustee only had about $7 million of equity on its balance sheet. Scarr then asked if the ASIC action could force Diversa into insolvency, and Plant said it had no letters of guarantee from its owners - a consortium comprising United States private equity interests and former Australian investment banker Matthew Kibble. Peterson said Diversa had allocated "north of $2 million" to defend the ASIC claim.
As the committee began to examine Peterson's controversial bonus for the 2025 financial year - the same period of the First Guardian collapse - Plant could be heard muttering "far out" into his microphone. He said the board believed Peterson had performed well as chief executive and had not considered replacing him.
Plant justified the bonus on the basis that "Diversa had nothing to do with the fraud" and there was "no link" between Peterson's performance and First Guardian, a comment that aggravated Labor senator Josh Dolega.
"Average punters would be absolutely disgusted with what you have just said," Dolega said.
Diversa acts as a third-party trustee that holds assets on behalf of superannuation funds to monitor risk and ensure compliance for clients.
Its largest clients are Superhero and Praemium. Both had consistently complained that their members were overcharged by Diversa but were blocked from finding a new trustee provider. Diversa, as trustee, could ultimately decide if a change was in the best interests of a fund's members.
Superhero publicly flagged its attempt to exit Diversa, the first major attempt to defect from the trustee, which will be closely watched by peers.
Peterson said previous applications from Superhero had yet to satisfy Diversa that they were in the members' best interest, at one point citing that the alternate provider, Super Trustees Australia, had just five staff members.
He argued that commercial interests were not a factor in discussions about trustee transfers. Diversa took on notice whether it had asked Superhero to provide a first aid policy to the trustee to justify the transition.
"It sounds harder to get out of than a marriage," O'Neill said.
